case_analysis.focal_point: Whether restitution imposed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act is a criminal punishment such that the Ex Post Facto Clause bars its retroactive application.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Ex Post Facto Clause) and the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA), Pub. L. No. 104-132, Title II, Subtitle A, 110 Stat. 1227 (codified primarily at 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that MVRA restitution is penal (i.e., part of the defendant’s criminal sentence) because it is imposed only following a criminal conviction, is mandatory for covered offenses, is administered and enforced through criminal-judgment machinery, and serves classic punishment purposes (retribution, deterrence, and incapacitation through supervision and sanctions for nonpayment). Because it is punishment, retroactive application of an MVRA amendment that increases or extends restitution obligations violates the Ex Post Facto Clause. Petitioner and supporting amici also contend that labeling MVRA restitution as merely compensatory ignores its statutory design and real-world operation (e.g., amounts and procedures not mirroring civil tort, limited victim control, and enforcement mechanisms that track criminal penalties).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States initially opposed certiorari and defended affirmance on the ground that even assuming MVRA restitution is a criminal penalty, the particular retroactive application at issue did not increase punishment in a way that triggers an Ex Post Facto violation. After certiorari was granted, the Solicitor General notified the Court that the government would not defend the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and would instead support petitioner on the limited question presented—i.e., the government’s merits position before the Supreme Court is that the Eighth Circuit’s reasoning on whether MVRA restitution is punishment should not be upheld, and the government filed a brief supporting vacatur on that question.
key_precedents: The Eighth Circuit decision below: United States v. Ellingburg, 113 F.4th 839 (8th Cir. 2024) (as referenced in petitioner’s brief materials)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that MVRA restitution is chiefly compensatory and therefore outside the Ex Post Facto Clause—still does not fit the statute’s design: it is triggered only by conviction, imposed at sentencing, entered in the criminal judgment, and enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms, which makes it function as punishment when retroactively enlarged. Justice Alito’s Hudson-first approach reinforces a minimalist path: we can resolve this case by holding that MVRA restitution, as Congress structured it, is punitive for Ex Post Facto purposes in the retroactivity posture before us, without announcing a categorical rule for all restitution regimes. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline strengthens the analysis by confirming our own repeated description of restitution as a criminal “penalty,” undercutting the claim that it is merely a civil debt. Institutionally, I would favor vacatur and remand to avoid entrenching the Eighth Circuit’s sweeping nonpunitive rationale, particularly given the government’s changed position.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that MVRA restitution is merely compensatory and so outside the Ex Post Facto Clause—fails under the Constitution’s original public meaning because this obligation is imposed only upon conviction, entered as part of the criminal judgment, and enforced through the criminal process; those are the hallmarks of punishment, whatever remedial benefits flow to victims. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on restitution’s integration into sentencing and penal enforcement confirms that we are dealing with a sanction annexed to the offense, not an ordinary civil debt. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline strengthens the textual and precedential footing: this Court has repeatedly described restitution as a criminal “penalty,” consistent with Congress’s own phrasing that restitution is imposed “in addition to … any other penalty.” On that understanding, a retroactive amendment that increases or extends restitution consequences aggravates punishment after the fact and falls within the Ex Post Facto Clause’s core prohibition.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—restitution is compensatory and thus “civil”—doesn’t survive Hudson/Ward’s focus on Congress’s design: the MVRA is conviction-triggered, imposed at sentencing, entered in the criminal judgment, and enforced through penal mechanisms, all of which look like punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes. Chief Justice Roberts’s suggestion of a narrow vacate-and-remand is persuasive institutionally, because we can reject the Eighth Circuit’s categorical “nonpunitive” rationale without opining on restitution in every constitutional setting. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline reinforces the step-one intent analysis: this Court has repeatedly described restitution as a “penalty,” which undercuts any attempt to recharacterize MVRA restitution as purely remedial here. On a practical-consequences view consistent with the Clause’s purpose, permitting retroactive enlargement of a sentence-integrated monetary sanction would invite after-the-fact increases in punishment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that restitution is compensatory and therefore civil—cannot override the MVRA’s actual design and coercive administration: it is conviction-triggered, mandatory at sentencing, embedded in the criminal judgment, and enforced through penal machinery, which is exactly where Hudson/Ward and Smith v. Doe tell us to look absent the “clearest proof” of a purely civil scheme. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on the statutory command that restitution be imposed “in addition to … any other penalty” is especially probative of punitive intent at step one, and Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline underscores that our own precedents repeatedly describe restitution as a criminal “penalty.” Chief Justice Roberts’s suggestion to proceed narrowly—vacate and remand given the government’s changed position—fits institutional prudence without diluting the core holding that retroactive enlargement of this sentencing sanction implicates the Ex Post Facto Clause. From a pragmatic perspective, the real-world burdens of criminal legal debt on indigent defendants make fair notice and restraint against after-the-fact increases in punishment indispensable here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is compensatory and therefore “civil,” but the MVRA’s text makes that label hard to sustain: § 3663A(a)(1) requires restitution only upon conviction and expressly directs that it be imposed “in addition to … any other penalty,” which is a strong textual marker that Congress integrated it into punishment rather than creating a freestanding civil remedy. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on restitution’s placement in the criminal judgment and enforcement through sentencing mechanisms bolsters the Hudson/Smith step-one inquiry: Congress designed MVRA restitution to operate as part of the sentence. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline matters for coherence—our own repeated description of restitution as a “penalty” undercuts a categorical nonpunitive characterization for Ex Post Facto purposes. Given those features, a retroactive increase or extension of this conviction-triggered obligation looks like an after-the-fact enlargement of punishment and should trigger Ex Post Facto scrutiny.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that restitution is compensatory and so “civil”—fails under the Hudson/Smith framework because Congress made MVRA restitution conviction-triggered, mandatory at sentencing, and entered in the criminal judgment, which is strong evidence of punitive design and operation. As the Chief Justice stresses, its embedding in the sentencing judgment and enforcement through penal mechanisms makes it untenable to treat the obligation as a freestanding civil remedy for Ex Post Facto purposes. Justice Kagan’s focus on the text requiring restitution “in addition to … any other penalty,” coupled with our descriptions of restitution as a “penalty” in Pasquantino and Paroline, reinforces that later amendments enlarging the obligation retroactively aggravate punishment. I therefore remain with petitioner: the Ex Post Facto Clause’s original public meaning forbids after-the-fact increases in consequences annexed to the offense.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that MVRA restitution is compensatory and therefore civil—still doesn’t fit the statute Congress enacted: restitution is conviction-triggered, imposed in the sentencing judgment, and enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms, which under Hudson/Smith are strong indicators of punishment absent the “clearest proof” otherwise. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on our own descriptions of restitution as a criminal “penalty” in Pasquantino and Paroline strengthens the step-one intent inquiry and makes it difficult to sustain the Eighth Circuit’s categorical “nonpunitive” framing. I also find Chief Justice Roberts’s institutionalist proposal persuasive: we can vacate and remand to reject the categorical reasoning and resolve this case without issuing a sweeping rule about restitution in all contexts. On that narrower disposition, retroactive application of an MVRA change that increases or extends the obligation functions as an after-the-fact increase in punishment barred by the Ex Post Facto Clause.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that MVRA restitution is compensatory and therefore outside the Ex Post Facto Clause—cannot overcome the statute’s text and original public meaning: a sanction imposed only upon conviction, included in the criminal judgment at sentencing, and enforced through penal mechanisms functions as punishment even if it has remedial aims. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the MVRA’s embedding in the sentencing scheme is decisive under a Hudson/Smith intent-focused inquiry and supports a narrow holding tied to this statutory design rather than a sweeping taxonomy of restitution in all contexts. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline matters because our own precedents repeatedly describe restitution as a criminal “penalty,” reinforcing that the ordinary meaning and doctrinal treatment align against a purely civil characterization for Ex Post Facto purposes. Accordingly, retroactive amendments that increase or extend MVRA restitution obligations amount to after-the-fact aggravation of punishment barred by the Clause.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that restitution is compensatory and therefore “civil”—fails to grapple with how the MVRA actually functions: it attaches only upon conviction, is imposed at sentencing, and is enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms that are coercive in ways indistinguishable from other criminal sanctions. Justice Sotomayor’s focus on the real-world burdens and enforcement consequences is especially persuasive under the Smith v. Doe intent–effects framework: even if Congress had remedial aspirations, the effects here are punitive enough that retroactive enlargement looks like an after-the-fact increase in punishment. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Pasquantino and Paroline matters because our own descriptions of restitution as a criminal “penalty” undermine the attempt to categorically segregate it from Ex Post Facto scrutiny. Chief Justice Roberts’s suggestion of a narrow vacate-and-remand fits my pragmatist approach: we can reject the Eighth Circuit’s categorical nonpunitive rationale without overresolving how restitution should be treated in every constitutional context.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause applies only to laws that impose criminal punishment, and the MVRA’s restitution scheme is embedded in the criminal sentencing process: it is triggered solely by conviction, mandated by 18 U.S.C. § 3663A, incorporated into the criminal judgment under § 3664, and enforced through criminal-judgment mechanisms. Under the Hudson/Smith intent-effects framework, Congress’s choice to make restitution a mandatory component of a defendant’s sentence is strong evidence of punitive intent, and at minimum the MVRA’s form and effects are not so clearly “civil” as to permit retroactive increases without constitutional scrutiny. Given the government’s abandonment of the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and the Court’s interest in institutional legitimacy, the narrow course is to vacate and remand rather than endorse an expansive holding that MVRA restitution is categorically nonpunitive for all purposes. On that limited question, I would treat MVRA restitution as criminal punishment sufficient to trigger Ex Post Facto concerns when applied retroactively to increase a defendant’s obligations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids Congress from enacting any law that retroactively “inflicts a greater punishment, than the law annexed to the crime, when committed.” Calder v. Bull, 3 U.S. (3 Dall.) 386, 390 (1798) (Chase, J.). Restitution under the MVRA, 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664, is imposed only upon conviction, is mandated as part of the criminal judgment, and is enforced through the sentencing court’s penal machinery—including supervision conditions and potential revocation—so it operates as punishment in the original public meaning sense attached to the criminal offense. Because it is penal in operation and effect, a retroactive change that increases or extends MVRA restitution obligations violates U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93, 99 (1997), the Ex Post Facto inquiry begins with statutory construction and Congress’s labeling and design choices. The MVRA is codified in Title 18, is triggered only upon criminal conviction, is imposed as part of the criminal judgment under 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A–3664, and is enforced through criminal-sentence mechanisms—features that strongly indicate Congress treated MVRA restitution as part of the criminal sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Even if one proceeded to the Mendoza-Martinez framework referenced in Smith v. Doe, 538 U.S. 84, 92–97 (2003), the “clearest proof” standard is unnecessary here because the statute’s structure and operation show it functions as penal. Because it is punishment, retroactive application that increases or extends restitution obligations runs into the Ex Post Facto Clause’s bar on increasing criminal punishment after the fact, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Restitution under the MVRA is imposed only upon criminal conviction, is mandatory for covered offenses, and is embedded in the criminal judgment and supervised/enforced through criminal mechanisms (18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664), all strong indicators that Congress created a penal sanction rather than a purely civil remedy. Under this Court’s intent-and-effects framework, we look first to whether Congress indicated a criminal label or purpose, and where (as here) the statute operates as part of the sentence, the Ex Post Facto Clause applies to bar retroactive increases in that financial punishment. See Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93, 99 (1997) (quoting United States v. Ward, 448 U.S. 242, 248, 251 (1980)) (statutory construction controls; only the “clearest proof” can override intent). Given the real-world burdens of criminal financial obligations—especially on indigent defendants and their families—allowing retroactive expansion would undermine fairness and the Constitution’s basic protection against after-the-fact increases in punishment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Smith v. Doe’s intent–effects framework, the MVRA is best read at step one as Congress’s instruction to impose restitution as part of the criminal sentence: it applies only upon conviction and directs courts to order restitution “in addition to . . . any other penalty” for covered offenses. See 18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1). The MVRA’s placement in the sentencing process and its enforcement through criminal-judgment mechanisms strongly indicate a penal design rather than a freestanding civil remedy, making the Ex Post Facto Clause applicable when later changes increase or extend the obligation. Even if one proceeded to step two, the mandatory, conviction-triggered deprivation enforced through penal supervision has sufficiently punitive purpose and effect to override any compensatory label.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The MVRA’s text makes restitution part of the criminal sentence: it directs courts to order restitution for covered offenses “in addition to … any other penalty,” 18 U.S.C. § 3663A(a)(1), and it is imposed only upon conviction through criminal-judgment procedures—strong indicators Congress meant punishment, not a freestanding civil remedy. Our cases likewise describe restitution as a criminal “penalty” imposed as part of the sentence, see Pasquantino v. United States, 544 U.S. 349, 365 (2005), and Paroline v. United States, 572 U.S. 434, 456 (2014), which reinforces the plain meaning and structure of the statute. Even under the Hudson/Mendoza-Martinez framework, restitution’s mandatory, conviction-triggered, and coercively enforced features make it punitive in effect, and any ambiguity about constitutional consequences should be resolved against retroactive penal increases consistent with the Ex Post Facto Clause. Because restitution under the MVRA is punishment, retroactive application of amendments that increase or extend the restitution obligation is barred.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Restitution under the MVRA is imposed only upon a criminal conviction and as part of the sentencing judgment, 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664, using criminal procedures and enforcement mechanisms—strong indicators that Congress meant it to function as a component of the criminal sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Applying the intent-effects framework of Smith v. Doe, 538 U.S. 84 (2003), the statutory context and placement in the criminal code point to punitive intent at step one, and in any event the effects (mandatory imposition, supervision, and sanctions tied to noncompliance) carry punitive hallmarks under the Mendoza-Martinez factors. Because the Ex Post Facto Clause bars retroactive increases in criminal punishment, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, a retroactive MVRA change that increases or extends restitution obligations cannot be applied to pre-enactment conduct. Vacating the Eighth Circuit’s contrary reasoning is also a practical, institutionally modest course given the government’s changed position and the need for administrable constitutional lines.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The MVRA’s text and structure treat restitution as part of the criminal sentence: it is imposed “in addition to … any other penalty” and is ordered at sentencing through the criminal judgment under 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A and 3664, using penal enforcement mechanisms. Under Smith v. Doe’s intent-effects framework (drawing on Mendoza-Martinez), Congress’s placement of restitution within the sentencing scheme and its mandatory, conviction-triggered operation strongly indicate a punitive character, at least for Ex Post Facto purposes. If the MVRA restitution obligation is punishment, retroactively applying an amendment that increases or extends that obligation would run afoul of the Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Given the government’s post-certiorari concession and the criminal-sentencing features reflected in the statutory text, I would vote to reverse/vacate the judgment below on the punishment question.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying the Smith v. Doe (Mendoza-Martinez) intent-effects framework, restitution under the MVRA functions as part of the criminal sentence: it is imposed only after conviction, mandated by statute for covered offenses, entered in the criminal judgment, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms under 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A and 3664. Those features provide strong evidence that Congress attached restitution to punishment rather than creating a freestanding civil remedial scheme, and in any event the effects are sufficiently punitive—coercive collection and sanctions tied to supervision and sentencing—to negate a purely compensatory label. Given the Ex Post Facto Clause’s core concern with retroactive increases in criminal punishment, retroactively applying an MVRA change that increases or extends restitution obligations is constitutionally problematic under U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Procedural fairness and practical consequences also counsel against allowing the government to enlarge sentencing exposure after the fact through a “civil” characterization that does not match how MVRA restitution actually operates.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether restitution imposed under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act is a criminal punishment such that retroactive application triggers the Constitution’s Ex Post Facto Clause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3 (Ex Post Facto Clause) as applied to restitution ordered under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA), Pub. L. No. 104-132, Title II, Subtitle A, 110 Stat. 1227.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that MVRA restitution is part of the defendant’s criminal sentence and operates as punishment (not merely civil compensation), so it must be treated as penal for Ex Post Facto purposes. Petitioner and supporting amici emphasize that restitution is imposed only after conviction, is mandatory in covered cases, is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, and historically has been used as a punitive sanction. Because it is penal, Congress cannot retroactively apply statutory changes that aggravate restitution consequences without violating the Ex Post Facto Clause.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government’s position evolved. In its certiorari-stage opposition, the United States defended affirmance of the judgment on the narrower ground that—even assuming MVRA restitution is a criminal penalty—there was no ex post facto increase in punishment on these facts. After certiorari was granted, the Solicitor General notified the Court that the United States will not defend the Eighth Circuit’s rationale and will instead support petitioner on the question presented (i.e., will argue that MVRA restitution is criminal punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes) and seek vacatur.
key_precedents: Ellingburg v. United States, 113 F.4th 839 (8th Cir. 2024) (decision below)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument remains that restitution is compensatory and thus civil, but that characterization cannot overcome the MVRA’s operative design: it is triggered only by conviction, imposed in the sentencing judgment, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms—features that make it function as punishment when applied retroactively to increase a defendant’s exposure. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Smith v. Doe’s intent-effects framework provides a narrow and institutionally prudent path: even if Congress invoked remedial aims, the effects here are sufficiently penal to implicate the Ex Post Facto Clause in this retroactivity setting. Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch’s citations to Bajakajian and Paroline reinforce (without requiring a broad holding) that our precedents have treated conviction-conditioned monetary exactions and restitution as punitive in relevant respects. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning point further supports that pecuniary sanctions attached to the criminal sentence fit within the historic concept of “punishment,” so I would hold only that the MVRA cannot be applied retroactively to make restitution more onerous.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that MVRA restitution is “compensatory” and thus not punishment—fails under the Constitution’s original public meaning because founding-era “punishment” encompassed pecuniary sanctions imposed as a consequence of criminal guilt, and the MVRA makes restitution conviction-triggered, part of the sentencing judgment, and enforced through criminal process. Justice Alito’s emphasis on how Congress integrated restitution into the criminal judgment reinforces that this is not an ordinary civil debt but a penal consequence attached to the offense. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan’s use of Smith v. Doe’s intent-effects framework is consistent with my approach here insofar as it confirms what the text and historical understanding already show: Congress cannot evade the Ex Post Facto Clause by labeling a sentence-imposed monetary exaction “remedial.” Colleagues’ citations to Paroline and Bajakajian, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett note, are not dispositive of original meaning but corroborate that this Court has recognized conviction-conditioned monetary exactions as punitive in relevant respects, so retroactive aggravation is barred.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—restitution is compensatory and thus not "punishment"—still fails against the MVRA’s text and operation: it is triggered only by conviction, imposed in the sentencing judgment, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, which under Hudson’s practical-effects inquiry are classic indicia of a penal sanction. Chief Justice Roberts’s intent-effects framing (drawing on Smith v. Doe) is persuasive because whatever Congress’s remedial rhetoric, the statute’s mandatory, conviction-conditioned design makes retroactive application that increases exposure functionally punitive. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning point reinforces that pecuniary exactions attached to a criminal sentence were historically understood as punishment, preventing Congress from evading the Ex Post Facto Clause by labeling. Justice Barrett’s citations to Bajakajian and Paroline further support treating conviction-tethered monetary obligations as punitive in relevant respects, so I see no legal basis to switch sides.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that MVRA restitution is “compensatory” and thus civil—cannot control where the obligation is triggered only upon conviction, imposed in the sentencing judgment, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms that can materially impair liberty and economic survival, especially for indigent defendants. Justice Kagan’s Smith v. Doe intent-effects framing sharpens the analysis: even if Congress invoked remedial aims, embedding mandatory restitution inside criminal sentencing is powerful evidence of punitive design and, at minimum, punitive effect when applied retroactively to increase exposure. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Bajakajian and Justice Gorsuch’s on Paroline strengthen (not weaken) the conclusion that conviction-tethered monetary exactions are recognized in our cases as punishment in relevant respects, bringing them within the Ex Post Facto Clause when retroactively aggravated. Consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional proposal, the holding can be narrowly limited to retroactive application that makes restitution more onerous, without sweeping pronouncements about all restitution regimes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—that MVRA restitution is purely compensatory and therefore regulatory—still doesn’t overcome the statute’s textual and procedural design choices: it is conviction-triggered, imposed in the criminal judgment at sentencing, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, which are powerful indicators of penal intent and effect under Smith v. Doe. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow framing is methodologically attractive to me: we can hold only that retroactive application that increases a defendant’s restitution exposure aggravates punishment, without reclassifying all restitution everywhere. Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Paroline and Bajakajian strengthens (rather than weakens) the conclusion that conviction-tethered monetary exactions can be “punishment,” making the “civil debt” characterization administratively and doctrinally incoherent in this ex post facto setting. Nothing in the compensatory rationale genuinely undermines the practical reality that Congress embedded this obligation inside sentencing, so treating it as punishment for retroactivity purposes best preserves statutory coherence and workable lines.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that MVRA restitution is “compensatory” and so outside the Ex Post Facto Clause—fails because constitutional meaning turns on a measure’s legal operation, not a label: this obligation is triggered only by conviction, imposed in the criminal judgment at sentencing, and enforced with criminal-justice tools, all classic indicia of punishment. Chief Justice Roberts’s Smith v. Doe intent-effects framing usefully confirms that even assuming mixed remedial aims, the mandatory, conviction-conditioned effects are penal in the relevant constitutional sense. Justice Thomas’s Calder-era original-meaning argument further strengthens the conclusion that pecuniary exactions attached to a criminal sentence were understood as “punishment,” foreclosing any reclassification as mere civil debt. Colleagues’ reliance on Bajakajian and Paroline (as Justice Barrett and others note) corroborates that our precedents treat conviction-tethered monetary exactions as punitive, so retroactive increases implicate ex post facto limits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that restitution is compensatory and therefore civil—does not square with the MVRA’s conviction-triggered, sentencing-integrated design and its enforcement through criminal-justice mechanisms; those features make it function as punishment when applied retroactively to increase exposure. Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrow holding is persuasive on institutionalist grounds: we can resolve only the ex post facto problem of retroactive aggravation without opining categorically about every restitution regime. Justice Thomas’s Calder/original-meaning point further reinforces that pecuniary sanctions imposed as part of a criminal judgment were historically understood as punishment, and colleagues’ reliance on Paroline and Bajakajian confirms our modern recognition that conviction-conditioned monetary exactions have punitive character. No compensatory label overcomes that history-and-structure reality under the intent-effects framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that restitution is compensatory and therefore not “punishment,” but the MVRA’s text and structure tie restitution to conviction and sentencing in a way that is dispositive under an original public meaning and our modern intent-effects cases. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Smith v. Doe is persuasive: whatever Congress’s remedial rhetoric, mandatory, conviction-triggered imposition in the criminal judgment and enforcement through criminal-justice mechanisms make the sanction punitive in effect when applied retroactively to increase exposure. Justice Thomas’s Calder-era framing strengthens that conclusion because founding-era “punishment” encompassed pecuniary sanctions imposed as part of the sentence, so retroactively aggravating that obligation fits squarely within the Ex Post Facto Clause. Colleagues’ citations to Bajakajian and Paroline do not cut the other way; if anything, they confirm that conviction-conditioned monetary exactions (including restitution) are treated as punishment in relevant constitutional contexts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent framing—that MVRA restitution is compensatory and thus civil—still does not answer the core procedural reality: the obligation is triggered only by conviction, imposed in the criminal judgment at sentencing, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms that materially constrain defendants, which is why retroactive expansion functions as aggravated punishment. Chief Justice Roberts’s Smith v. Doe intent-effects approach is persuasive here because Congress’s labels cannot override effects that are inextricably tethered to guilt and sentencing administration. Justice Sotomayor’s point about the real-world burdens on indigent defendants reinforces my pragmatic concern that allowing retroactive increases would let Congress intensify penal consequences through sentencing machinery while evading the Ex Post Facto Clause’s fairness constraint. Colleagues’ reliance on Paroline and Bajakajian (as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett note) corroborates that conviction-conditioned monetary exactions are treated as punishment in our cases, so I see no doctrinal basis to reclassify this as mere civil debt for Article I purposes.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, forbids retroactive laws that increase criminal punishment, and the MVRA’s restitution is imposed only upon conviction and as part of the criminal judgment—features that strongly indicate a penal sanction rather than a purely civil remedy. Under Smith v. Doe’s intent-effects framework, even if Congress labeled restitution as compensatory, the “effects” here—mandatory imposition in covered cases, operation through criminal sentencing, and enforcement through criminal-justice mechanisms—are sufficiently punitive to treat MVRA restitution as punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes. Given the government’s post-certiorari alignment with petitioner and the need for a narrow, legitimacy-preserving resolution, the Court can hold only that retroactive application of MVRA provisions that make restitution more onerous is impermissible where it increases the defendant’s penal consequences. That approach respects precedent and avoids broader pronouncements about restitution in other statutory contexts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids Congress from retroactively increasing the "punishment" for a completed offense, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, and under the original public meaning reflected in Calder v. Bull, 3 U.S. (3 Dall.) 386 (1798), "punishment" encompassed sanctions imposed as part of the criminal sentence for public wrongs, including pecuniary penalties. Restitution under the MVRA is imposed only upon conviction, mandated as part of the sentencing judgment in the federal criminal code, and enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, so it operates as a criminal punishment rather than a mere civil debt. Because restitution so imposed fits the founding-era understanding of penal consequences, a retrospective application that aggravates the defendant’s restitution exposure triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause and cannot stand. The Eighth Circuit’s contrary view in Ellingburg v. United States, 113 F.4th 839 (8th Cir. 2024), conflicts with this original meaning and should be vacated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause applies to measures that increase “punishment,” and under Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93, 99 (1997), the analysis begins with statutory construction—whether Congress indicated the sanction is criminal. The MVRA’s restitution is imposed only upon conviction, is ordered as part of the sentencing judgment, and is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, all strong textual and structural indicators that Congress treated it as a penal component of the sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Even if characterized as partly compensatory, its mandatory, offense-triggered operation and integration into the criminal judgment make retroactive application that aggravates the defendant’s obligation an unconstitutional increase in punishment under U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Practical consequences also counsel against letting Congress evade ex post facto limits by relabeling sentencing consequences as “restitution” while using criminal enforcement tools.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: MVRA restitution is imposed only after conviction and as part of the sentencing judgment, 18 U.S.C. §§ 3663A, 3664, and is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms; in operation it functions as a penal consequence, not merely a private compensatory remedy. Under the Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, Congress may not retroactively increase the punitive consequences attached to past conduct, and mandatory restitution that attaches to the conviction is a classic way the State exacts a sanction. The MVRA’s own retroactivity clause—applying to pre-enactment offenses only “to the extent constitutionally permissible,” MVRA § 211, 110 Stat. 1241—signals awareness that Ex Post Facto limits are implicated if restitution is punitive in effect. The Eighth Circuit’s contrary approach in Ellingburg v. United States, 113 F.4th 839 (8th Cir. 2024), undervalues the real-world burdens imposed on defendants and the punitive character of a mandatory, court-ordered monetary obligation entered as a criminal sentence.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying Smith v. Doe’s two-step framework, the MVRA’s restitution scheme is best read as part of the criminal sentence Congress attached to conviction, because it is imposed at sentencing through criminal procedures and enforced with criminal-justice mechanisms, not as a freestanding civil regulatory program. That placement and operation supply the clearest indicator of congressional intent at step one, making restitution "punishment" for Ex Post Facto purposes under U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Treating MVRA restitution as penal also promotes statutory coherence and administrability: courts already calculate and enter restitution as a sentencing component alongside incarceration and fines, and retroactivity rules should track that reality. Even if one proceeded to step two, the Mendoza-Martinez factors (including traditional aims of punishment and the sanction’s linkage to conviction) point in the same direction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids retroactive laws that increase “punishment,” U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3, and MVRA restitution bears the ordinary hallmarks of a criminal sanction: it is imposed only “at the culmination of a criminal proceeding,” requires conviction, and is part of the sentence. This Court has treated monetary exactions as punishment when conditioned on criminal guilt, see United States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321, 328 (1998), and it has described restitution as meting out “criminal punishment,” Paroline v. United States, 572 U.S. 434, 456 (2014). Because the MVRA makes restitution mandatory and enforces it through criminal-justice mechanisms, it is not merely a civil remedial device; retroactive application that aggravates the restitution consequences therefore triggers ex post facto scrutiny. Any remaining ambiguity about the statute’s penal character should be resolved against retroactivity consistent with the Constitution’s fixed meaning and traditional lenity-like constraints on punitive impositions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Restitution under the MVRA is imposed only upon conviction and as part of the criminal judgment at sentencing, and it is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms (including the prospect of additional criminal consequences for noncompliance), all of which strongly indicate Congress tied it to the penal process rather than creating a freestanding civil remedy. Applying the Smith v. Doe intent-effects framework, Congress’s placement of mandatory restitution within the criminal sentencing scheme and its mandatory, conviction-triggered operation reflect a punitive design that at minimum renders it “criminal” in effect even if characterized as compensatory. Treating MVRA restitution as nonpunitive would also be difficult to square with Ex Post Facto Clause doctrine’s historical focus on preventing retroactive increases in the consequences attached to a crime, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3. Given those features and the need for a workable rule consistent with history and tradition, retroactive application should trigger Ex Post Facto scrutiny because MVRA restitution functions as criminal punishment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Ex Post Facto Clause forbids retroactive laws that “increase the punishment” for a crime, and the MVRA’s restitution is imposed only “at the culmination of a criminal proceeding” upon conviction, a hallmark of punishment rather than a purely civil remedy. Under Bajakajian, a monetary exaction tied to a criminal conviction and imposed in personam “constitutes punishment,” and this Court has similarly described restitution as meting out “criminal punishment” in Paroline. The MVRA also operates as part of the criminal sentence and is enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, reinforcing its penal character notwithstanding its compensatory aim. Given those textual and structural features, retroactive application that worsens restitution consequences triggers Article I, §9, cl. 3.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Restitution imposed under the MVRA is ordered only “at the culmination of a criminal proceeding” and depends on a conviction, making it functionally part of the criminal sentence rather than a freestanding civil remedy. Under this Court’s punishment analysis—looking to Congress’s design and the sanction’s operation, see Hudson v. United States (1997)—the MVRA’s mandatory, conviction-triggered, court-imposed restitution, enforced through criminal-justice mechanisms, has unmistakable penal characteristics and practical punitive consequences for defendants. That conclusion aligns with our recognition that monetary exactions tied to conviction are “punishment,” as in United States v. Bajakajian (1998), and with Paroline v. United States (2014)’s description of restitution as meting out “criminal punishment.” Accordingly, retroactive application that increases restitution consequences for pre-enactment conduct triggers the Ex Post Facto Clause, U.S. Const. art. I, § 9, cl. 3.
